Lessons.Title: More Symmetry
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Determine and justify every nonidentity rotation that maps a given figure onto itself, including its centre, directed angle and rotational order.
Verbal diagram: a regular pentagon centred at O has five vertices at equal 72-degree sectors; a rectangle centred at O has two pairs of opposite equal edges but unequal side lengths.

Student task: compare a regular polygon, non-square rectangle and non-equilateral isosceles triangle; list rotation angles and provide a counterexample. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct centre, permitted nonidentity angle, full-figure mapping, and sound justification. The original student-created poster and oral comparisons are human scored.
Independent Edulytiks teaching aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), CC BY 4.0. Original publisher artwork and restricted assessment materials are not reused.

16.1 source equivalent Which One Doesn't Belong: discuss original non-square rectangle, square, three-blade motif and isosceles triangle. Justify competing symmetry criteria, rather than identify unverified publisher pictures.

16.2 source equivalent Self Rotation: groups define a regular polygon, non-square rectangle or asymmetric triangle; mark ALL nonidentity rotations with centre, angle and direction, plus one invalid rotation. Square: 90,180,270 degrees; regular pentagon: 72,144,216,288; non-square rectangle: 180; non-equilateral isosceles triangle: none. Never count 0 or 360.

16.3 source equivalent Parallelogram Symmetry: parallelogram A(0,0),B(4,0),C(5,2),D(1,2) has centre M=(2.5,1). Half-turn about M exchanges A↔C, B↔D and fixes the figure set; a generic oblique parallelogram has no reflection axis. Optional infinite frieze patterns can have nonzero translational symmetry; finite bounded polygons cannot.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rotation symmetry
KeyConcepts.Definition: A nonidentity rotation about a point that takes the entire figure back onto itself.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check a common centre and full-figure vertex correspondence; rotations by a full 360-degree turn alone do not count.
KeyConcepts.Example: A non-square rectangle has 180-degree rotational symmetry, but not 90-degree rotational symmetry.

KeyConcepts.Title: Order of rotational symmetry
KeyConcepts.Definition: Number of distinct rotations through a full turn that map a shape to itself, including identity when counting order.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For a regular n-gon, the smallest positive such turn is 360/n degrees.
KeyConcepts.Example: A regular pentagon has order 5 with steps of 72 degrees.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rotation versus reflection
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rotation preserves the orientation of labelled vertices; a reflection reverses it.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Distinguish a turn about a centre from a mirror across a line.
KeyConcepts.Example: A non-equilateral isosceles triangle has a reflection axis but no nontrivial rotation symmetry.

WorkedExamples.Title: Regular pentagon
WorkedExamples.Question: Give all nonidentity rotational symmetries of a regular pentagon about its centre.
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide one complete revolution into five equal central sectors.
Steps: A regular pentagon has five equally spaced vertices around its centre.
The smallest turn taking each vertex to its next is 360/5=72 degrees.
Successive turns 72,144,216,288 degrees permute all vertices without changing the polygon.
The 360-degree turn is identity, not a nontrivial rotational symmetry.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each allowed turn maps the set of all vertices onto itself.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rectangle but not square
WorkedExamples.Question: Which turns of a 6-by-2 rectangle about its centre are symmetries?
WorkedExamples.Method: Test the positions and orientations of unequal sides.
Steps: A 180-degree turn swaps opposite corners and preserves all four sides.
A 90-degree turn sends a horizontal length-6 side to a vertical direction where the rectangle has length 2.
Thus quarter-turns do not map the rectangle to itself.
A full 360-degree rotation is identity, leaving 180 degrees as the nontrivial turn.
WorkedExamples.Check: The 90-degree turn would become valid if the rectangle were a square.

WorkedExamples.Title: A figure with reflection but not rotation symmetry
WorkedExamples.Question: Does triangle A=(-2,0),B=(2,0),C=(0,3) have a nonidentity rotational symmetry?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the uniqueness of an unmatched apex and the side-length pattern.
Steps: The equal sides AC and BC meet at unique apex C, while side AB has a different length.
Any symmetry of the triangle must map the unique apex C to itself.
A nonidentity rotation in the plane fixes only its centre, so its centre would have to be C.
Such a rotation cannot exchange A and B while retaining the other lengths and preserve the entire triangle; the triangle is not equilateral.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No nonidentity rotation maps this triangle to itself.
WorkedExamples.Check: Reflecting across x=0 does map it to itself, so reflection symmetry and rotation symmetry differ.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Counting a full 360-degree turn as evidence of nontrivial rotational symmetry.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Every figure maps to itself under identity, so this does not distinguish symmetric shapes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Find a strictly positive turn less than 360 degrees that preserves the entire figure.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming one symmetric-looking vertex is enough.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The whole set of vertices and edges must coincide with the original.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify the image of every defining vertex under the same centre and angle.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: Determine and justify every nonidentity rotation that maps a given figure onto itself, including its centre, directed angle and rotational order.
Mathematical hypotheses and vertex/figure correspondence must be checked before a symmetry or congruence claim.
Teacher-scored evidence is required for constructed diagrams, argument critique and original written explanations.

Lessons.Title: Working with Rigid Transformations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Give a systematic point-by-point sequence of rigid motions that aligns corresponding vertices of congruent figures and explain why each step preserves already matched points.

Verbal diagram: imagine two congruent, labelled triangles. A translation places the first named vertex on its target; rotation about that target aligns the second; optional reflection in their connecting line aligns the third when orientation is reversed.

Student task: give a word-only alignment procedure and analyse one invalid correspondence. Teacher rubric (0–4): true matching lengths, preserved previously matched vertices, precise motion order and reasoned third-vertex result; source card sorting and oral explanation are human scored.
Independent Edulytiks teaching aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), CC BY 4.0. Original publisher artwork and restricted assessment materials are not reused.

Source 17.1 Math Talk From Here to There: given a segment AB with perpendicular bisector CD, mentally identify a reflection across CD that swaps A and B, or a half-turn about AB midpoint, and a half-turn about CD midpoint that exchanges C and D. Students justify the named centres/mirrors and note that C and D need not be symmetric about AB unless separately specified.

Source 17.2 Card Sort: teacher gives FOUR separate original paper cards: a translation of a triangle, a mirror reflection, a rotation with named centre and a two-step composition. Students first sort by number of motions, then re-sort by orientation preserved/reversed, explaining both systems, and label an exact pointwise sequence for every rigid pair. The optional investigation may compare a genuine glide reflection with a single reflection/rotation/translation without claiming every composition reduces to one motion.

Source 17.3 Reflecting on Reflection: to find an exact mirror line taking P to P' for distinct corresponding points, construct the perpendicular bisector PP'. Check that every other corresponding vertex pair shares that SAME line. A proposed guessed line or a perpendicular bisector of the wrong correspondence is not proof.

First-party complete pointwise alignment: A(0,0), B(2,0), C(0,1) map to D(5,3), E(5,5), F(4,3). Translate by A→D=(5,3), then rotate 90 degrees CCW about D. A' stays D, B' reaches E and C' reaches F; the first pair stays fixed while matching the second. If the third vertex is on the opposite side of matched line DE, reflect in DE without changing D or E.

KeyConcepts.Title: Point-by-point alignment
KeyConcepts.Definition: A method using translation, rotation and optionally reflection to map named corresponding vertices to their target positions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: First map A onto D by translation, then rotate about D to align B with E, then reflect across line DE only if the third vertex is opposite the target side.
KeyConcepts.Example: Congruent triangles ABC and DEF with valid correspondences can be aligned through at most three such rigid motions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed-point-preserving step
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rotation about D fixes D; reflection about line DE fixes both D and E.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Choose later motions that preserve previously aligned points.
KeyConcepts.Example: After A reaches D and B reaches E, a reflection in DE can interchange the two sides without moving D or E.

KeyConcepts.Title: Congruence hypotheses
KeyConcepts.Definition: A valid correspondence is constrained by equality of matching side lengths/angle measures.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Verify AB=DE, AC=DF, BC=EF before asserting the third vertex must match.
KeyConcepts.Example: A proposed matching that swaps unequal sides cannot be achieved by rigid motions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Align congruent triangles
WorkedExamples.Question: Triangle ABC has A=(0,0), B=(2,0), C=(0,1). Target DEF has D=(3,2), E=(3,4), F=(2,2). Give a rigid sequence.
WorkedExamples.Method: Translate A to D; rotate about D counterclockwise by 90 degrees.
Steps: Rotate the translated image 90 degrees counterclockwise about D.
Vector DB=(2,0) rotates to (0,2), so B→E=(3,4).
Vector DC=(0,1) rotates to (-1,0), so C→F=(2,2).
All corresponding vertices now coincide; no reflection is required.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Translate by (3,2), then rotate 90 degrees counterclockwise about D.
WorkedExamples.Check: Distances AB=DE=2, AC=DF=1 and BC=EF=√5 agree.

WorkedExamples.Title: Align mirror-image triangles
WorkedExamples.Question: A=(0,0),B=(2,0),C=(0,1); D=(3,2),E=(5,2),F=(3,1). Which rigid motions suffice?
WorkedExamples.Method: Translate and then reflect across the target base line.
Steps: Translate by (3,2) so A→D, B→E and C→(3,3).
Line DE is horizontal y=2; reflection across y=2 fixes D and E.
Reflect (3,3) across y=2 to (3,1)=F.
All named vertices match and the final figure is congruent.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Translate by (3,2), then reflect across line DE (y=2).
WorkedExamples.Check: A bare translation is insufficient for the third vertex because its orientation is reversed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a false correspondence
WorkedExamples.Question: Can a rigid motion map A=(0,0),B=(2,0) to D=(0,0),E=(3,0) with A→D and B→E?
Steps: Measure AB=2.
Measure DE=3.
Every rigid motion preserves the distance between its two mapped points.
Since AB≠DE, no rigid motion can satisfy both A→D and B→E.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, the assigned point correspondence is impossible.
WorkedExamples.Check: A drawing that visually looks similar does not override the distance-preservation invariant.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Aligning the second vertex by a new translation that displaces the first matched vertex.
CommonMistakes.Correction: After placing A at D, rotate about D so D remains fixed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reflecting across a line not through the two already aligned vertices.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Reflection may disrupt the two fixed correspondences.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use line DE itself for an optional final reflection.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: Give a systematic point-by-point sequence of rigid motions that aligns corresponding vertices of congruent figures and explain why each step preserves already matched points.
Mathematical hypotheses and vertex/figure correspondence must be checked before a symmetry or congruence claim.
Teacher-scored evidence is required for constructed diagrams, argument critique and original written explanations.

Lessons.Title: Practicing Point by Point Transformations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Describe, draw and check a sequence of rigid motions that maps an entire figure to a target while avoiding specified obstacles throughout the continuous motion.
Optional source lesson, intended to provide further transformation practice after U01:L17. Unlike an endpoint-matching problem, an obstacle course adds time-dependent constraints and boundaries.

Student task: draw a movable triangle on a map of obstacles, submit every intermediate image and a path-clearance argument. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct motions, endpoint correspondence, continuous collision verification, clear readable diagrams; don't auto-grade a coordinate pair as proof of a safe entire-figure route.
Independent Edulytiks teaching aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), CC BY 4.0. Original publisher artwork and restricted assessment materials are not reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intermediate image
KeyConcepts.Definition: An intermediate figure after each stage of a rigid motion sequence, before the final target image.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Draw or list every intermediate vertex position; endpoint-only checks do not establish a collision-free route.
KeyConcepts.Example: A triangle may reach the target by a direct translation that crosses an obstacle even if endpoints are clear.

KeyConcepts.Title: Collision-free motion
KeyConcepts.Definition: A continuous physical path in which the moving figure never intersects forbidden obstacles or leaves allowed bounds.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check the swept figure for all parameter values along each translation or rotation.
KeyConcepts.Example: A line segment translated from x=0 to x=4 intersects an obstacle spanning x∈[2,3] even if start/end lie outside it.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sequential precision
KeyConcepts.Definition: Motion steps require a directed length, rotation centre, angle and order sufficiently precise to reproduce the figure's path.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Specify each motion and label images after each step.
KeyConcepts.Example: T(x,y)=(x+3,y), then quarter-turn about (3,0), yields a different path from the reverse order.

WorkedExamples.Title: An obstacle-crossing translation
WorkedExamples.Question: A point marker at (0,0) must reach (4,0), but a forbidden vertical barrier covers x between 2 and 3 at y=0. Is a direct right-4 translation safe?
WorkedExamples.Method: Parameterize the continuous segment traced by the point.
Steps: Direct translation path is P(t)=(4t,0) for 0≤t≤1.
At t=1/2, P=(2,0), which is on the barrier.
The start (0,0) and endpoint (4,0) are outside the barrier but the path is not.
Use a sequence of vertical and horizontal translations around a bounded barrier if a safe corridor exists.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; the direct translation intersects the forbidden region.
WorkedExamples.Check: A point demonstration is only a necessary check for a shape; the entire moving figure requires collision review.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two-stage path around a rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: A point travels from (0,0) to (4,0), with forbidden rectangle 2≤x≤3 and −1≤y≤1. Give a safe path.
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose a vertical clearance greater than 1 before moving horizontally.
Steps: Translate up 2 to (0,2).
Translate right 4 to (4,2), staying at y=2, outside the forbidden rectangle.
Translate down 2 to (4,0).
Each segment avoids the rectangle because the vertical legs have x outside [2,3] and the horizontal leg has y>1.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Up 2, right 4, down 2 safely routes the point.
WorkedExamples.Check: For a triangle instead of a point, its full footprint must fit the clearance; a 2-unit point clearance may not suffice.

WorkedExamples.Title: Verify a two-step rotation and translation
WorkedExamples.Question: Translate P=(1,0) right 2, then rotate it 90 degrees counterclockwise about O=(0,0).
Steps: Translation sends P to (3,0).
A 90-degree counterclockwise rotation about O sends (3,0) to (0,3).
The final distance to O equals the intermediate radius 3; the translation itself need not preserve distance to O.
The path differs if the rotation is performed before the translation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Checking the final image alone is insufficient to certify obstacle avoidance.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Approving a collision-free path merely because final and initial drawings do not overlap the obstacle.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An intermediate point or part of the figure can cross a forbidden region.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the whole swept figure during each continuous motion.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a solution for one vertex and assuming the full polygon fits the corridor.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Other vertices can collide even while the tracked vertex avoids obstacles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Test all edges and the polygon interior against each obstacle at every stage.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: Describe, draw and check a sequence of rigid motions that maps an entire figure to a target while avoiding specified obstacles throughout the continuous motion.
Mathematical hypotheses and vertex/figure correspondence must be checked before a symmetry or congruence claim.
Teacher-scored evidence is required for constructed diagrams, argument critique and original written explanations.
